newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU stability pact seen delayed until '97.
newsitem.headline: EMU stability pact seen delayed until '97.

text.p: German insistence on a tough budget stability pact among countries forming a common currency has led European Union officials to scale back their predictions for a full agreement this year.

Instead, they now say EU leaders will only agree a broad political statement in favour of a pact at the European Council in Dublin on December 13 and 14. The hard details will carry over until next year.
"It's not going to be done by December," said one official familiar with the deliberations of the EU's monetary committee.

In spite of rising optimism over the pace of negotiations on a pact that would fine countries running budget deficits above three percent of total output, EU monetary officials say Germany is set to reiterate its demands for much tougher accord.

The EU's monetary committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, is due to gather for a regular meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday and will discuss the budget pact along with other issues related to economic and monetary union.
"It is very well possible that in Dublin there will be a political declaration of the stability pact and the legal text will be adopted next year," said another senior EU official.
One of Germany's primary objectives is to lay out the precise economic conditions under which a country running an excessive deficit would avoid sanctions.
After an intense debate in October, the European Commission backed away from defining the so-called exceptional economic conditions when it unveiled its proposal for the budget accord.
Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy had initially proposed an annual decline of 1.5 percent in gross domestic product but met strong resistance from several other commissioners.
Germany, meanwhile, had initially proposed a two percent decline in GDP over four consecutive quarters.
In Bonn, Peter Hausmann, spokesman for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said the main points of a stability pact could still be agreed by December.

Yet officials and analysts say there is a growing perception in Germany that a single currency will be purchased at the expense of budgetary rigour. Such worries have political implications which financial markets and other EU countries have failed to realise.

"The watering down of the language in the stability pact and the acceptance of doubtful accounting practices is creating the feeling in Germany that we have to watch that the Maastricht criteria is not being undermined," said Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

In particular, some pointed to the widespread and misguided view that Kohl will ignore recent criticisms voiced by those in Bundesbank and German government in order to secure a single currency by 1999.
"It's beyond belief that the criticism will be ignored by Kohl," said another EU official.
"The real point is that within his own party he will have major problems if we go into 1998 and people think all of this is fudged," he added.

While most believe the odds are still in favour of the single currency being launched on time in 1999, markets should not assume that Kohl would abide by the timetable to the detriment of his own political fortunes, they added.
